title: Valencia’s floods show why a GDP rebound can coexist with lasting losses
summary: Soledad Núñez estimates that the October 2024 flash floods reduced Spanish GDP growth in the fourth quarter of that year by only 0.1–0.2 percentage points. Some estimates nevertheless put lost wealth in Valencia province above €17 billion, equivalent to more than 20% of its 2023 GDP. These figures describe different geographic areas, economic quantities and reference periods. The second uses one year’s provincial production as a scale for a loss of assets. It is not an estimate that provincial GDP fell by a fifth. Núñez’s January 2026 speech uses that distinction to explain how reconstruction can raise measured activity after a disaster while households and firms remain substantially poorer. She also records the human cost of close to 230 deaths (pp. 1–2).

The initial shock reduced both the resources available for production and the volume of transactions. Restricted mobility prevented commuters reaching work. Damaged roads and railways interrupted deliveries, while diversions around motorway closures increased delays and production costs. Damage to tourism facilities and beaches reduced reservations. Some residents lost access to bank services or held damaged cash. These mechanisms operated in different sectors and over different periods. While the interruption to production flows registered in GDP, destruction of an existing home, vehicle, factory or piece of public infrastructure reduced the owner’s stock of wealth immediately. A national growth number dilutes a geographically concentrated disaster and cannot capture that stock adjustment.

Reconstruction subsequently supports spending. Households replace appliances and vehicles, and repairs generate demand for construction and professional services. Public measures included direct aid, guarantees for firms and moratoria on loan payments. Insurance compensation was another source of financing. Spain’s Consorcio covers certain extraordinary risks on insured persons and property, funded primarily through surcharges on standard insurance premiums. By January 2026, the speech reports more than 250,000 claims and €4.1 billion reimbursed in connection with the floods. The payment total concerns this insurance mechanism. It neither measures the total loss nor shows how much of the remaining loss was met by other transfers or households’ own resources (p. 2).

The banking evidence similarly requires care with denominators. The central bank estimates that the disaster affected €27 billion of credit, split between €17 billion to households and €10 billion to non-financial companies. Together these exposures were 2.1% of national lending to those two sectors. Affected credit is the balance exposed to the event; it is not an estimate of loan losses. Lending stocks in affected areas rose significantly in the subsequent months, while non-performing loans increased moderately from December 2024. Both outcomes can occur as borrowers need funds to restore assets and a subset faces difficulty servicing existing debt. The central bank found limited effects at national level and no evidence of systemic banking risk. Smaller and more local institutions were more affected, although none required exceptional measures. Núñez credits public support with helping the financial sector absorb the shock (pp. 2–3).

Over a longer horizon, the net effect on productive capacity remains open. Asset destruction can leave a household or business with weaker finances and less access to credit. Some businesses may close, reducing local productive capacity as well as spending power. Among survivors able to refinance, new equipment could be more productive than the equipment destroyed. Núñez illustrates this possibility with investment in automation. It is a conditional channel, not an empirical finding about realised productivity in Valencia. A rebound in spending on replacements therefore gives incomplete information about regional economic potential and the distribution of losses.

For a central bank, the episode illustrates both an operational responsibility and a measurement problem. Banco de España coordinated access to cash, including exchange of damaged notes through bank branches and mobile outlets. It also compared credit volume and quality in affected and other areas, drawing on data shared by several institutions. For future stress tests, sector-specific damage functions need to allow for geographic variation, infrastructure and supply-chain disruption. Granular observations of past losses are scarce. For investors applying the Valencia case elsewhere, adaptation, insurance coverage, the speed of transfers and the concentration of lending are conditions that determine how a physical shock reaches credit quality. The reported national outcome cannot be transferred mechanically to another region or insurance system (pp. 3–4, note 1).

questions.question: How much of the increase in lending financed productive rebuilding, and how much bridged a cash shortfall?
questions.detail: Both would increase credit outstanding, but only the former directly expands productive capacity. Match loan-level purpose, maturities and moratorium use to insurance receipts, reopening dates and investment in affected municipalities. The Banco de España study in note 1 is the natural starting point. The distinction matters for projecting repayment and earnings once emergency support expires.

questions.question: Which lenders retain the greatest loss exposure after guarantees and insurance?
questions.detail: The €27 billion figure measures affected balances, with losses likely to vary across lenders and borrowers. Obtain local exposure concentrations, loan-to-value distributions, insurance coverage, guarantee terms and subsequent arrears for similar borrowers inside and outside the flood zone. A regional bank credit assessment needs the timing of recoveries as well as the eventual loss borne by the bank.

questions.question: Does replacement investment ultimately offset business exits and lost household wealth?
questions.detail: The speech establishes a mechanism and an example of technological upgrading, but supplies no estimate of the long-run net gain. Track capital spending, firm survival, employment and productivity against comparable regions over several years, allowing for pre-existing trends. A construction upswing alone could otherwise be mistaken for a persistent improvement in the tax base or the creditworthiness of local firms.
